title: Make the benchmark helper measure the work

blocks.text: The team settles performance arguments with `MicroBench`, a small helper of its own, because JMH isn't on the build's class path. Last week it reported that the new coupon check costs 0.02 ns per call, and that the old one, which nobody had touched, had become three times slower after someone raised the number of warm-up rounds. Nobody believes either number.

Write `measure(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/MicroBench.java`. It gets the work, the inputs to call it with, and the number of warm-up rounds; it runs the work over every input in each warm-up round and then in one timed round. The report it returns gives:

items: `nanosPerCall`: the time per call of the timed round;
`checksum`: the sum of every value the work returned.

blocks.text: When you're done, the numbers describe the work as it would run in production, whatever the JIT is allowed to do with the loop. About seven lines.
The tests pass a clock of their own, so no test depends on how fast the machine is.

cases.says: with no warm-up, the report gives the clock's elapsed time divided by the number of inputs
the work runs once per input in every warm-up round and in the timed round
every value the work returns, in the timed round too, is added to the checksum
the timed round passes each input in turn rather than repeating one value
the clock is read after the warm-up rounds, so the time per call is that of the timed round only

origin.section: A Benchmark Measures Nothing When the JIT Can Drop the Work or Fold Its Input

concepts: A call whose input never changes can be computed once, so a benchmark must vary its inputs as production does.
A benchmark that times its first rounds measures the compiler's work, so the timing starts after the warm-up.
A loop whose results nobody uses can be deleted by the JIT, so it measures nothing; every result must reach something the JIT can't see through.
